title: VPC graceful upgrade anchors & TF adapters (working notes)
body:
Purpose:
- Capture a lightweight pattern for performing VPC/network upgrades with minimum blast radius for tenant private deployments (VPC, on-prem gateway, TGW attachments).
- Introduce the concept of "upgrade anchors" (small immutable pieces we pin/hand off) plus Terraform adapter patterns to enable in-place and blue/green upgrades without tearing customer-facing connectivity.

Scope / constraints:
- Applies to private deployments where customer networking is managed by the onboarding team (Redwood-managed TF) and changes may touch: route tables, NATs, TGW attachments, subnets, ingress/egress ACLs, VPN/Direct Connect/XConnect.
- Does NOT cover full infra replacement (k8s clusters, disks) — focused on network control plane + connectivity fabric.
- Must work with both cloud VPC (AWS/GCP/Azure) and on-prem edge gateways; adapter layer should be provider-agnostic where possible.

Key concept: Upgrade anchors (short explainer)
- Definition: a small set of network objects we treat as "anchored" (pinned identity/attachment) during upgrades. Anchors serve as stable touchpoints for routing and handoffs so we can change surrounding config without breaking customer traffic.
- Typical anchors: bastion/NAT instance(s) (or NAT gateway attachment), TGW/VPC attachment IDs, VPN peer resource IDs, core route table(s), primary egress ACLs.
- Anchor rules:
  - Anchors must have explicit lifecycle rules in TF (prevent_destroy / create_before_destroy where supported).
  - Anchors should be the minimal set to preserve tenant reachability; everything else is allowed to be replaced behind the anchor.

Why anchors help:
- Keeps external attachments stable (carrier circuits, TGW attachments), avoids propagating new attachment IDs to customer configurations.
- Enables blue/green for routing: swap route targets to new subnets/attachments instead of replacing the attachment.
- Simplifies rollback: restore route table reference to previous anchor target.

Terraform adapter pattern (notes):
- Problem: many customers/customers' infra have naming/ID assumptions; TF changes often force resource replacement (new attachment IDs).
- Adapter = thin wrapper module that exposes a stable "anchor_id" and hides provider id churn. Internally it manages reconciliation and can opt into: in_place, attach-new-and-swap, or create-new-and-drain.

Module interface (example):
- module "tgw_anchor" {
    source = "github.com/redwood-inference/tf-modules//vpc-anchor"
    name = var.name
    preferred_subnet = var.preferred_subnet
    replacement_strategy = var.replacement_strategy # inplace | swap | blue_green
    lifecycle_policy = { prevent_destroy = true }
  }

Implementation notes:
- Use lifecycle.prevent_destroy only for anchor identity resources (attachments, primary route tables). Avoid global prevent_destroy — it blocks reconciliation and provokes manual intervention.
- For AWS TGW attachments: create new attachment in separate module output, then update route table referencing logic to switch target via small change set (no delete of old attachment until traffic drained).
- For on-prem: wrap carrier HLD metadata in TF variables (circuit_id, vlan_tag) and treat the circuit as anchor_id for routing references.

Upgrade sequences (opinionated, safe default):
1) Pre-checks and snapshot
   - Run terraform plan with -out to capture change set.
   - Snapshot TF state (terraform state pull -> store in object store along with plan).
   - Validate HELM/k8s networking dependencies (if any) — ensure endpoints referencing old subnets have healthchecks.
2) Stage new pieces behind anchors
   - Apply new resources (new subnets, new ENIs, new NATs) in staging TF workspace (or separate module instance).
   - Confirm internal connectivity and control-plane (SSH, control plane API).
3) Swap routes to anchors (traffic cutover)
   - Update primary route table target from old resource to new resource ID.
   - Monitor traffic metrics (per-route flow logs / VPC flow / packet counters) for 15–30 min.
4) Validate and drain
   - Validate application health (end-to-end synthetic checks and customer smoke tests).
   - Gradually drain and disable old resources; do NOT destroy until stable for 24–72 hours depending on SL.
5) Cleanup (final apply)
   - When stable, perform final TF apply to remove old resources. Keep anchor prevent_destroy policy until Customer sign-off.

Rollback guidance:
- Precondition: we have a saved plan and state snapshot.
- Rollback steps (fast-path):
  1) Update route tables back to previous anchor target (single change apply).
  2) Re-enable old NAT/gateway if it was disabled.
  3) Revert TF workspace to state snapshot and apply smaller plan to restore original resource counts.
- If plan fails to reapply: escalate to SRE for state surgery. Keep documented runbook for tainting vs state-object edits.

Testing matrix (quick):
- Unit: TF module unit tests using terratest or kitchen-terraform for module interface and lifecycle behaviors.
- Integration: create an ephemeral tenant account and run full upgrade sequence; include e2e synthetic checks and path tests for both internal and external egress.
- Canary: route 5–10% of traffic to new path for 2 hours before full cutover.

Operational checkpoints & metrics to watch:
- Connectivity: packet loss, TCP RST rate, connection setup latency to common endpoints.
- Control-plane errors: API throttles, attach/detach errors in cloud provider logs.
- Billing/Cost: transient double-NAT charges, cross-AZ data transfer during parallel paths.
- User impact: error rates on authentication, timeouts.

Handoff checklist (SE -> Customer Ops / NetOps):
- Share plan and state snapshot location+versions.
- Confirm anchor list and ownership (who can approve prevent_destroy removal).
- Provide rollback command snippets and expected time-to-restore.
- Run through DR test case: complete a cutover and rollback in a lab tenant.

Terraform module notes / gotchas:
- Provider differences: GCP has different replace semantics for routes -> prefer route table rewrite vs resource replacement.
- Avoid implicit dependencies: use explicit depends_on for anchors to make change sets predictable.
- When using create_before_destroy, ensure downstream resources can handle temporary duplicates (e.g., two NATs).
- State drift: external network changes by customers (manual console edits) will cause diffs. Recommend enabling drift detection and alerts before any upgrade window.

Field examples / short pseudo-code (anchor adapter):
- resource "aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment" "anchor" {
    lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
    subnet_ids = var.subnet_ids
  }
  output "anchor_id" { value = aws_ec2_transit_gateway_vpc_attachment.anchor.id }

- adapter module should expose an "anchor_id" output and a "swap_target(resource_id)" small helper in docs.

Risk register (top items):
- Carrier/XConnect expected downtime if anchor incorrectly replaced. Mitigation: manual lock + change window.
- Provider API rate limits during parallel operations. Mitigation: paced concurrency and backoff.
- Cost spikes during parallel path period. Mitigation: pre-approve budget delta and notify finance/CS.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How long should we keep old resources by default? (24h/72h/7d) => propose 72h for high-risk customers, 24h for low-risk.
- Should anchors be tenant-level or account-level? some partners prefer account-level anchors for simplified ops.
- Implement a small TF hook to auto-create a "change-ticket" tag that links to JIRA for traceability.
- Need an internal script to automatically capture plan + state and upload to GCS/S3 with secure ACLs.

Next steps (actionable):
- [ ] Prototype adapter module for TGW/VPC attachment (PR #312 as starting point).
- [ ] Run one lab upgrade with the "swap" strategy on staging tenant (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Draft SE handoff checklist doc and include sample rollback CLI snippets (owner: Carlos).
- [ ] Add automated plan+state capture step to onboarding pipeline (owner: Priya).

Notes / references:
- See linked PR for tf-modules sample: GITHUB PR #312.
- Slack thread for recent outage postmortem that motivated anchors: #private-deploys (thread ts:1678912345).
- Confluence: PD-420 contains traffic-acceptance test matrix and synthetic checks definitions.

Informal thoughts (scratchpad):
- We should try not to over-index on prevent_destroy — it becomes an operational footgun. Anchors are better enforced by process (ownership + tags) with a small number of prevent_destroy cases.
- A small UI in console to show "current anchor IDs" per tenant would reduce accidental replacements.

End of notes.
